extracted.intended_audience: advertisers, marketers, compliance officers, and consumer protection lawyers
extracted.subtask_description: Federal Trade Commission guidance and representative enforcement standards for advertising across categories (weight-loss, environmental, tobacco, alcohol, computer products, infomercials), describing what claims, disclosures, formats, and substantiation practices are required or unlawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantiation for health/efficacy claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers must possess adequate substantiation for efficacy and health-related claims (e.g., claims that products can treat, prevent, or reverse disease, or cause weight loss without diet and exercise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly references enforcement actions challenging unsubstantiated disease and efficacy claims for dietary supplements and other products (e.g., ephedra, DHEA, shark cartilage, hoodia, etc.). Remedies include consent orders, injunctions, and monetary redress. Examples: MaxCell BioScience (DHEA claims), Natural Heritage (essiac tea cancer claims), multiple weight-loss cases. In practice, advertisers need competent and reliable scientific evidence before making such claims; otherwise enforcement (and large redress/judgments) can follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety disclosures for hazardous ingredients
rubrics_metrics.description: When products contain ingredients with known risks (e.g., ephedra, androgens/steroids), advertisers must disclose safety risks prominently in labeling and advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement orders have required disclosures of risks such as breast enlargement, testicle shrinkage, infertility, increased facial/body hair, voice deepening, clitoral enlargement, and other safety warnings. Examples: Met-Rx/AST Nutritional Concepts orders requiring labeling/advertising disclosures for steroid-like supplements; Global World Media (ephedra) requiring safety disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: No disease-treatment/prevention claims without approval/substantiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Products and supplements may not be advertised as treating or preventing diseases (e.g., cancer, AIDS/HIV, diabetes) unless substantiated or otherwise lawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple consent orders challenge claims that products cure or treat serious diseases (e.g., Natural Heritage, Nutrivida, Body Systems Technology). Such claims invite FTC enforcement and large remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endorsements and testimonials must disclose material connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers must disclose material financial connections between advertisers and endorsers, and must not use deceptive consumer testimonials or expert endorsements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases cited (e.g., Chinery, Cytodyne, Xenadrine EFX) challenged deceptive consumer testimonials and failure to disclose material connections. The infomercial section also warns about deceptive expert endorsements/testimonials and requires the same level of substantiation as other media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deceptive before-and-after or performance claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that a product alone will produce dramatic physical changes (e.g., fat/inch loss, well-defined muscles, replacement for exercise) are deceptive unless supported by evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include electronic abdominal belts and topical creams (Telebrands, Ab Force, Abtronic, Fast Abs). The FTC has required redress and injunctive relief where such claims were unsupported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear and conspicuous disclosures; do not hide material terms in fine print
rubrics_metrics.description: Material cost, performance, or limitation information must be disclosed clearly and prominently, not buried in inconspicuous fine print.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (Gateway, Dell, Micron, Palm, WebTV) challenged burying material cost/limitations in fine print. Specific examples include hidden telephone charges for 'free' or flat-fee internet services and fine-print disclaimers about required hardware or limited availability of features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free trials and billing practices must be truthful and cancellable
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotions for 'free' or trial services must disclose true costs, contract terms, and must honor cancellations (no continuing billing after cancellation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: America Online, Prodigy, CompuServe, Juno cases challenge deceptive free trial offers and continuing billing. Netpliance and other cases required refunds and disclosure of additional fees; failure to comply has led to civil penalties and redress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental marketing claims must be accurate and specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims using terms such as degradable, biodegradable, recyclable, recycled, refillable, ozone-safe/friendly, or general 'environmentally safe' must be truthful, and advertisers must make clear whether the claim applies to the product, the packaging, or a component.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Guides for the Use of Environmental Marketing Claims (16 C.F.R. § 260) interpret Commission caselaw and provide definitions and examples. The Guides emphasize clear, prominent qualifiers/disclosures and accuracy of comparative claims. The FTC announced reviews and held conferences on carbon offsets, RECs, and green packaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recyclability/biodegradability claims contingent on available facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that a product or packaging is recyclable or biodegradable are deceptive if, in practice, few or no recycling/composting facilities exist to handle the item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative cases (LePage's, Keyes Fibre, Archer Daniels Midland, Mobil Oil) challenged recyclable/biodegradable claims where appropriate infrastructure was lacking. Marketers should ensure infrastructure exists and disclose limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative environmental claims must be accurate and not misleading
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative statements about environmental benefits must be accurate and supported; qualifiers and disclosures must be clear and prominent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Environmental Guides address comparative claims explicitly. Cases challenging misleading comparative statements are cited; advertisers should avoid vague or unsupported superiority claims (e.g., 'environmentally friendly' without substantiation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy savings/performance claims must disclose tradeoffs and be substantiated
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that products save energy or improve performance must be accurate and disclose any relevant tradeoffs (e.g., less light output), and cannot omit material facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases against Osram Sylvania, General Electric, Castrol, Dura Lube, and others show enforcement where energy-saving or performance claims were misleading or omitted material limitations. Remedies include consent orders and penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tobacco advertising must comply with statutory warning and placement rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Cigarette and smokeless tobacco advertising and packaging must include health warnings in conspicuous, legible, and prominent form consistent with federal statutes and regulations (e.g., 15 U.S.C. § 1337; 15 U.S.C. § 4401; 16 C.F.R. § 307).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative cases (Stoker, R.J. Reynolds, Santa Fe Natural Tobacco) challenged failures to place required warnings or deceptive claims like 'no additives' implying safety. The Commission also publishes tar and nicotine ratings and reports to Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid implying a product is safer when it is not
rubrics_metrics.description: Marketers must not suggest a product is safer than others (e.g., 'no additives' cigarettes) unless the claim is accurate and not misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.J. Reynolds and related consent orders required disclaimers where 'no additives' claims might mislead consumers into believing a product is safer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alcohol marketing best practices to limit underage exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Industry is urged to adopt practices to avoid promoting alcohol to underage consumers: establish independent complaint boards, raise the audience composition standard for ad placement above ~50% adult, restrict campus/spring-break sponsorships, block underage website access, and limit placements in media with large underage audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FTC Report to Congress recommended these steps after evaluating self-regulatory efforts. The FTC also launched education/outreach initiatives (e.g., dontserveteens.gov). These are policy recommendations and represent enforcement priorities and encouragements to industry self-regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer/internet product claims must accurately describe capabilities and fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about built-in features (e.g., wireless Internet access), upgradeability, and cost structures must be accurate; additional hardware/software requirements and extra fees must be disclosed clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases against Palm, Hewlett-Packard, Microsoft, Gateway, WebTV, Netpliance, and others required clear disclosure of optional/required add-ons, additional phone charges, upgradability limitations, and refunds for incurred charges. Misrepresentations have led to consent orders and monetary relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warranties, leases, and money-back guarantees must disclose material terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotions for warranties, lease offers, or money-back guarantees must accurately represent the terms and not omit material limitations or requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gateway, Dell, Micron, and Gateway 2000 cases challenged misleading money-back guarantee and lease advertising. The Consumer Leasing Act and FTC enforcement have been applied to internet, print, and TV ads that conceal material costs or conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infomercial transparency: disclose commercial nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Program-length commercials (infomercials) must not mislead consumers about the format — viewers should know the program they are watching is a commercial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page states: 'Deceptive format: Do consumers know that the program they are watching is a commercial?' The FTC has brought many cases challenging deceptive infomercial formats and ordering remedies and injunctions (e.g., Kevin Trudeau, Window Rock Enterprises).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infomercial substantiation parity and compliance with other consumer rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Infomercial advertisers must meet the same substantiation standards as other media and must comply with consumer rules such as the Mail Order Rule and Telemarketing Sales Rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The infomercial section explicitly states: 'Infomercial advertisers must possess the same level of substantiation that would be required to support claims disseminated in any other media.' Other violations (Mail Order Rule, Telemarketing Sales Rule, unauthorized use of credit cards, unordered merchandise) have been core enforcement themes in infomercial cases.
